newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FOCUS-Ringgit firms, Malaysia swipes at speculators.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Ringgit firms, Malaysia swipes at speculators.

text.p: The Malaysian ringgit rebounded strongly on Monday after the authorities moved to prevent any further speculative pressure on the currency with a mild form of capital controls.
The move to limit non-trade swap transactions saw the ringgit rally to 2.5800 per U.S. dollar from Friday's late level of around 2.6350 but later it settled around 2.6030.
This together with the news the Thai government talks with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) were "going well" helped Asian currencies across the board.

The long-awaited package from Thailand is expected to get cabinet approval this week and finance minister Thanong Bidaya was upbeat. On emerging from seven days of talks with the IMF one reporter remarked that he looked sad.
"You call this face sad? I'm smiling," Thanong told the reporter. "I am confident it's going to be approved by the cabinet and it's going to be good news."
Thailand is braced for a fairly painful austerity package and IMF demands might be hard to swallow.
"The most painful issue will be related to disclosure," Russell Kopp, head of research at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson in Bangkok, told Reuters Financial Television.

"A flexible currency and capital exchange controls, those will have to go, but the real issue at the heart of these problems is political reform and a great part of what the IMF will do here is pry open disclosure."
The onshore baht firmed to 31.550 per dollar from Friday's late 31.750 with the offshore rate at 31.550 against 31.85.
In Malaysia, Bank Negara, the central bank announced that from Monday local banks have to limit non-trade-related currency swaps with overseas customers to $2.0 million.

A swap is an exchange of fixed interest payments in one currency for those in another, in this case the U.S. dollar and the Malaysian ringgit, with a commitment to exchange the principal amount at the end of the swap agreement at a set rate.
By imposing a $2.0 million ceiling, overseas players will be limited in the amount of ringgit they can obtain, thereby limiting the scope for speculation.
The move helped the ringgit but hit investor confidence on the stock market where prices of blue-chip issues fell sharply.

"I don't think the move in itself will have too much impact but what people are worried about is that it could put Malaysia a step back in terms of trying to be a financial centre," said Chaing Yao Chye, head of Asia Pacific research at CIBC in Singapore.

Also, Malaysia's move may be seen as a little over the top given that since the beginning of July, when pressure really started to mount on Asian currencies, the ringgit's fall has been far from spectacular and certainly not in the Thai baht's league.
The ringgit has come down only 3.0 percent on the dollar since July 1 and a lot of that must be due to the fact that the dollar itself has been firm around the world.
Since July 1 the yen has fallen over 3.0 percent against the dollar and the deutschemark has dropped 6.0 percent.

The Indonesian rupiah was underpinned by tight money market liquidity on Monday but trade was slow, with interest centered on the swap market where players were wary of Indonesia imposing controls similar to those announced by Bank Negara.
But traders thought that unlikely at this stage and noted that of all the Asian currencies the rupiah had weathered the recent storm well.
"Indonesia has a policy to liberalise exchange controls as much as they can and they have already widened the intervention band," said one trader at a European bank in Singapore.
"President Suharto has made it pretty clear that he is happy with the liberal system that's in place for the rupiah."
Spot rupiah was a little firmer at 2,595.00 per dollar against Friday's late 2,604.00.

The Taiwan dollar ended slightly firmer but was below an earlier high on continued heavy demand for dollars. Taipei dealers said central bank intervention on Saturday signalled that the authorities thought there had perhaps been enough of a correction.

It was at T$28.654 after opening at T$28.631 against Saturday's T$28.705 close. The Taiwan dollar tumbled more than four percent last week after the central bank gave up on its long-standing defence of the T$28 level.

The Philippine peso was expected to firm as banks needed to sell dollars to improve their liquidity after the central bank ordered a two percentage point increase in liquidity reserves to curb speculation last week.
One Manila trader said the central bank had sold $1 million at 29 pesos in Monday's first deal. The peso was at 29.00 per dollar against its previous close of 28.99.
